s: A. Free Exercise.
"Congress shall make no law… prohibiting the free exercise" of religion.
The baseline.

Employment Division v. Smith (1990) held that a neutral, generally applicable law burdening religious practice (there, a peyote ban applied to Native American Church members) does not require strict scrutiny.
This replaced the compelling-interest test of Sherbert v. Verner (1963) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) outside the unemployment-compensation context.
When strict scrutiny still applies.
Lack of neutrality.
The law targets religion or shows hostility to it: Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah (1993, ordinances targeting animal sacrifice); Masterpiece Cakeshop (2018, commission hostility).
Lack of general applicability.
The law has a mechanism for individualized exemptions (Fulton v. Philadelphia, 2021), or treats any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious exercise.
Comparability is judged by the risk the government interest addresses (Tandon v. Newsom, 2021).
Exclusion from public benefits because of religious status or use violates free exercise (Trinity Lutheran, 2017; Espinoza, 2020; Carson v. Makin, 2022).
Hybrid rights (Smith dicta), such as free exercise combined with parental rights.
Mahmoud v. Taylor (2025) held that parents are entitled to notice and opt-outs where school instruction substantially interferes with their children's religious upbringing.
Church autonomy and the ministerial exception.
Religious institutions choose their ministers free of employment-discrimination law (Hosanna-Tabor, 2012; Our Lady of Guadalupe, 2020).
Statutory protection.
The Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993) restores strict scrutiny against the federal government (Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, 2014; Tanzin v. Tanvir, 2020, damages available).
RLUIPA protects prisoners and land use (Holt v. Hobbs, 2015).
Title VII requires accommodating employees' religion unless doing so imposes "substantial increased costs" (Groff v. DeJoy, 2023).
Free Exercise.
Is a sincere religious exercise burdened?
Is the law neutral?
Look for targeting, hostility, or a gerrymander.
Is it generally applicable?
Look for individualized exemptions or comparable secular activity treated more favorably.
If either fails: strict scrutiny (compelling interest, narrowest means).
If both hold: rational basis under Smith.
Then check RFRA (federal), RLUIPA, and state RFRAs.
Church autonomy or the ministerial exception may bar the claim entirely.
